source.title: Systematic Investigation of Sparse Perturbed Sharpness-Aware Minimization Optimizer
source.authors: Peng Mi; Li Shen; Tian-He Ren; Yi-Yi Zhou; Tian-Shuo Xu; Xiao-Shuai Sun; Tong-Liang Liu; Rong-Rong Ji; Da-Cheng Tao

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and supplementary materials; some figure text is garbled, but the extracted table results are legible.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAM's sharpness-based training approach as the basis for its proposed sparse perturbation method and comparator, then reports SSAM's performance. Its results do not test the listed claim versions about memorization, width, architecture, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy for SSAM against SAM and SGD. These optimizer results are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure a behavior named by V1–V8. Cited results about large-batch training and flat minima are not this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization premise to develop and evaluate sparse SAM. It does not test any listed version: its sharpness analyses do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance against training–test error gaps, and its optimizer comparisons concern SAM variants rather than adaptive methods versus SGD.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the authors' conclusion: sparse perturbations can retain competitive or better SAM accuracy while offering efficiency gains, with results depending on mask pattern and implementation. Actual acceleration is demonstrated for the specialized N:M ViT implementation; Table 10's explicit unstructured SSAM timings are slower than full-data SAM.
record.recipe_differences: SSAM retains SAM's perturbed-loss training approach but masks the perturbation using either Fisher information or a dynamic sparse mask; perturbation patterns and implementation are varied.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with dataset, perturbation sparsity, mask-generation method, mask structure, and explicit versus implicit implementation. The paper reports larger drops at higher sparsity on ImageNet and with structured masks.

fits_no_version.finding: At 50% perturbation sparsity, ResNet18 SSAM-F/SSAM-D attain 96.81%/96.87% on CIFAR10 versus SAM's 96.83%, and 81.24%/80.59% on CIFAR100 versus 81.03%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse SAM can preserve or improve SAM test accuracy, with outcomes depending on dataset and mask method.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.7 reports flatter filter-normalized training-loss landscapes for SSAM and dominant Hessian eigenvalues of 82.6, 26.2, and 19.4 for SGD, SAM, and SSAM, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse SAM can reach flatter training-loss landscapes than SGD and SAM on ResNet18/CIFAR10 under the paper's landscape and Hessian measures.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The reported table results give test accuracy but not training error or a train–test gap. No uncertainty estimates are stated for these values. Some landscape and Hessian comparisons are figure-only and do not quantify a gap.
record.rows_left_out: Other test-accuracy entries for additional sparsities, models, datasets, and mask structures appear in Tables 1–5 and 7–10. They are omitted because these results concern the same sparse-SAM performance finding and the six rows retain the core 50% sparsity comparisons plus the contrasting outcomes across datasets and mask methods.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance random-label held-out accuracy. Partial label corruption is evaluated only through clean test accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning. Adam is used in the ViT timing experiment without this comparison.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes. Using fewer samples for perturbation calculation does not change the update batch size.
Dropout addition or removal and its interaction with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance as a correlate of training–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, including ranking against norm and margin measures. Filter-normalized landscape plots and Hessian spectra do not establish these comparisons.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No listed-version verdict follows from the landscape plots, Hessian spectra, or conditional PAC-Bayesian bound. These do not measure V7's specified empirical relationship. The six recorded accuracy rows are numerically correct but belong under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD on held-out performance under specified tuning.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, including small training sets and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a correlate of the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
